title: Why Deception Pass runs at eight knots
teaches: Currents driven by a difference in level, and why slack water comes after high water
summary: **A tidal current in a narrows runs downhill.** The water flows from the side where the sea stands higher to the side where it stands lower.

**The two ends of Deception Pass get their tide by different routes.** Rosario Strait gets it straight from the Strait of Juan de Fuca, while Skagit Bay sits at the end of a long way round and fills partly through the pass itself.
**A level difference of about a metre is enough for eight knots.** Water falling a height h reaches a speed of about √(2gh), less what friction takes.
**Slack water comes after high water, not at it.** The current stops when the two levels are equal, which is when the basin behind the gap reaches its own high water.
**A narrower gap runs faster but carries less.** The basin behind it rises and falls less and later, so the difference across the gap grows.
**Eight knots comes only with the biggest tides.** Spring tides and the larger of each day's two tides make the biggest difference; on most tides the peak is lower.
**Admiralty Inlet works differently.** It is wide and deep, so the levels on its two sides stay close, and its current is the volume the whole Sound needs to rise and fall.
**Tide tables and current tables are separate for a reason.** The time of high water does not tell you when the current turns.

blocks.text: In the spring of 1792 George Vancouver's two ships, HMS *Discovery* and HMS *Chatham*, spent weeks charting the inland waters behind the Strait of Juan de Fuca. The ships anchored and the work was done from open boats, rowed and sailed for days at a time into every inlet. Early in June one of those boat parties, led by Joseph Whidbey, the *Discovery*'s master, worked north up the long channel east of a large wooded shore that Vancouver had taken to be a peninsula joined to the mainland. Near its northern end the channel did not close. It led into a narrow, rock-walled gap, and through the gap to the open water of the Strait.[^whidbey]

The "peninsula" was an island. Vancouver named it Whidbey's Island for the man who had found the way round it, and he named the gap Deception Passage, because the coast had fooled them: from the west, among the rocks and islets, the opening is easy to take for a small bay.

The gap is Deception Pass, and since 1935 a bridge has crossed it high above the water. Stand on that bridge at the right hour and the water below runs like a river in flood, with standing waves, boils and whirlpools, at speeds that on the biggest tides reach eight **knots**, about 15 km/h or 9 mph.[^knot] Many small boats cannot make headway against it. An hour or two later the same water lies still, and then it starts running the other way.

Out in the open Sound a few miles away, the tide lifts and lowers the water gently, and a swimmer barely feels it move. Something about this gap turns the gentle tide into a torrent, and it has to do with where the water stands on each side of it.

blocks.caption: Deception Pass, between Fidalgo Island to the north and Whidbey Island to the south. Pass Island splits the gap in two; the bridge crosses both channels by way of it.

blocks.text: Lesson 2 measured a river by its **discharge**, the volume that passes each second: width times depth times speed. A river runs because its bed slopes. Water at one end stands higher than water at the other, and gravity pulls it down the slope.

A tidal current in a narrows is the same thing, sideways. If the sea on one side of a gap stands higher than the sea on the other, water pours through from the high side to the low side. The current does not care about the level on either side by itself, only about the difference between them, and the bigger the difference, the faster the water runs.

The speed follows from the size of the drop. Water that falls through a height *h* picks up the same speed as a stone dropped from that height: about √(2*gh*), where *g* is 9.8 metres per second per second. A drop of one metre gives about 4.4 metres a second, or eight and a half knots. Some of that speed is lost to friction against the rock and to the eddies that tumble off the walls of the pass, so a real gap needs a little more than a metre to reach eight knots.[^torricelli] A metre is not much. It is a few steps down a staircase. But spread across a gap less than 200 metres wide, it drives one of the fastest tidal currents in the state.

Both sides of Deception Pass are part of the same Salish Sea, yet the sea can stand a metre higher on one side than the other, because the tide reaches the two ends by different routes. Lesson 10 showed the tide as a long wave moving into the inland waters from the Pacific. The western end of the pass opens onto Rosario Strait, which takes the tide almost straight from the Strait of Juan de Fuca. The eastern end opens onto Skagit Bay, which sits at the far end of a long way round: in through Admiralty Inlet, past the southern tip of Whidbey Island, and up Possession Sound and Saratoga Passage. That route is long, and the high water travelling along it arrives later and differs in height. Skagit Bay also takes water through the pass itself, and the pass is far too small to keep up.

blocks.task: Step through to the last stage

stages.label: The pass
stages.text: Deception Pass joins Rosario Strait, to the west, to Skagit Bay, to the east. Its western end is a short way from the open Strait of Juan de Fuca.

stages.label: The short way
stages.text: The tide comes in from the Pacific along the Strait of Juan de Fuca and turns north into Rosario Strait. The western end of the pass rises and falls with the Strait.

stages.label: The long way
stages.text: To reach Skagit Bay by water the tide must go in through Admiralty Inlet, round the south end of Whidbey Island and north up Saratoga Passage. Along this route it arrives later and at a different height.

stages.label: A difference
stages.text: The two ends of the pass rise and fall at different times and by different amounts. At times the Strait side stands a metre or more above Skagit Bay, and at others below it. The pass runs downhill between them.

blocks.text: Most people who live near salt water carry a picture of the tide in which high tide and still water go together: the tide comes in, stops at the top, and goes out. On an open beach that is close enough. In a narrows it is wrong, often by an hour or more, and the figure below shows why. It is a model with the same parts as Deception Pass: a sea on one side whose level rises and falls with the tide, a gap, and a bay on the other side that, in the model, can only fill and empty through the gap. Before you play it, guess.

blocks.caption: Two basins joined by a narrows, through one tide. A model: one tide of the same size each half day, and a bay that fills only through the gap.
blocks.task: Guess, then play the tide on past high water until the current stops

blocks.text: At high water on the Strait side the current is still running in. It is slowing, but it is far from stopped. The reason is in the levels. All through the rising tide the bay has lagged behind the sea, because the gap can only pass so much water each second. When the sea outside reaches its highest and starts to fall, the bay is still lower, so water keeps pouring in. The bay goes on rising until the falling sea and the rising bay meet. At that moment, and only then, the two levels are equal, and the current stops. That is **slack water**. It comes at the bay's own high water, which is later than the sea's. Then the sea is the lower of the two, and the pass starts to run out.

The misconception has a name among sailors, who learn the hard way that a tide table and a current table are two different books. The tide table gives the times of high and low water; the current table gives the times of slack and of the strongest flow. At a narrows like Deception Pass they can be far apart. Reading the two tables is the subject of the field branch (F1).

Now try the width of the pass. Make it wide, and the bay keeps up with the sea: the two levels rise and fall almost together, the difference across the gap stays small, the current is gentle, and slack comes close to high water. Make it narrow, and the bay can't keep up. Its tide grows smaller and later, the difference across the gap grows, and the water in the gap runs faster, even though less of it gets through in all.

The other slider is the size of the tide outside. A bigger tide means a bigger difference across the gap and a faster current. Lesson 8 showed the range swelling and shrinking twice a month, from spring tides to neaps, and lesson 9 showed that in the Salish Sea the two tides of each day are unequal, one large and one small. Put those together and the strongest currents in Deception Pass come on the large tide of the day, near springs, on the days when lesson 9's inequality makes one tide of the day especially large. Those are the tides that run at eight knots or a little more. On an ordinary day the strongest flow is a few knots less, and on the small tide of a neap day the pass is tame by comparison.[^mixed]

**An estimate** of the water that goes through. The main channel is less than 200 metres wide and a few tens of metres deep, so call its cross-section 4,500 square metres. At the peak of a big flood the water runs at about 4 metres a second, so the discharge, lesson 2's width times depth times speed, is about 18,000 cubic metres a second. That is more than twice the average flow of the Columbia at its mouth. The flood doesn't hold that peak for long; averaged over the six hours or so that it runs, the speed is nearer 2.5 metres a second. Over a whole flood that comes to 4,500 × 2.5 × 22,000 seconds, about a quarter of a cubic kilometre: a lake a kilometre square and 250 metres deep, poured through a gap you could throw a stone across, and then poured back.

blocks.text: The rule of the gap also explains why the current is slowest just when it is turning. Near slack the two levels are almost equal, and a difference of a few centimetres drives only a slow drift. That is why divers, kayakers and boats wait for slack to go through, and why the window is short: as soon as the levels pull apart again, the water picks up speed.
Every basin of the Sound is joined to the next by a narrows, and each has its own current. They don't all work the same way.

**Tacoma Narrows** is the door to South Sound. Everything south of it, from Carr Inlet to Olympia's Budd Inlet, fills and empties through a channel about a mile wide. South Sound is large and its tide is the biggest in the region (lesson 10), so a great deal of water must pass each tide, and the Narrows runs at several knots.

**Admiralty Inlet**, between Whidbey Island and the Quimper Peninsula near Port Townsend, is the main door of the whole Sound. It is several kilometres wide and deep, so it is a good door, and the levels on its two sides never get far apart. Its current is not mainly a fall from one level to another. It is simply the volume the Sound needs to rise and fall, squeezed through the doorway. A rough estimate: the Sound inside covers a little over 2,000 square kilometres; call it 2,000, and on a large tide it rises about 3 metres in about six hours. That is 6 cubic kilometres in 22,000 seconds, nearly 300,000 cubic metres a second. Divide by a doorway about 6 kilometres wide and 50 metres deep on average, and the water must move at about a metre a second on average, faster at the peak: a few knots.

Admiralty Inlet and Tacoma Narrows have something else in common. Each is a **sill**, a shallow rise in the floor between deeper basins, left by the glaciers that carved the Sound (the Geology course tells that story). The tide drags the whole column of water back and forth over these rises at a few knots, and the water tumbles and churns as it goes. That stirring at the sills will turn out to matter a great deal for what lies in the basins behind them, which is lesson 12's subject.

blocks.caption: Four narrows of Puget Sound and what drives each current.

spots.name: Deception Pass
spots.text: A small gap between two sides that get the tide by different routes. A level difference of up to a metre or more drives up to eight knots on the biggest tides.

spots.name: Admiralty Inlet
spots.text: The Sound's main door, several kilometres wide, with a sill about 60 metres down. The levels on each side stay close; the current is the volume the Sound needs to fill and empty, a few knots.

spots.name: Tacoma Narrows
spots.text: The door to South Sound, about a mile wide, with the region's biggest tides behind it. Several knots, and a sill that stirs the water.

spots.name: Rich Passage
spots.text: A winding gap between Bainbridge Island and the Kitsap shore, the way into Sinclair Inlet and Bremerton. The Seattle to Bremerton ferries go through it.

blocks.text: **Outdoors.** Deception Pass State Park is about an hour and a half north of Seattle. Look up the day's current predictions for Deception Pass (NOAA publishes them; F1 shows how to read them) and go twice: once near the strongest flood or ebb, and once near slack. Walk out on the bridge each time and watch the same water. At full flow it will be streaked and boiling, with whirlpools spinning off Pass Island and a visible tilt in the surface through the narrowest part. At slack it will be glassy. Then look up the tide prediction for a station nearby and see how far apart high water and slack really were that day.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: The current in a narrows follows the difference in level across it, not the level on one side.
Slack comes when the levels are equal, which is after high water outside.
A narrow gap runs fast because the basin behind it cannot keep up.

blocks.caption: Six questions on currents in a narrows
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: What drives the fast tidal current through a narrows such as Deception Pass?
choices: The water stands higher on one side of the gap than the other, and runs downhill
The Moon pulls the water directly through the gap as it passes overhead
Wind blowing down the Strait piles water into the gap twice each day
items.why: The tide reaches the two ends at different times and heights, so a level difference builds up across the gap and the water runs from the high side to the low.

items.ask: At a narrows between the sea and a bay that fills through it, when is slack water?
choices: When the levels on both sides are equal, which is after high water outside
At the moment of high water outside, when the tide stops rising
Exactly halfway between high water and low water outside
items.why: The bay lags the sea. At the sea's high water the bay is still lower, so the flood keeps running until the bay catches up.

items.ask: If a narrows were made narrower, what would happen to its current?
choices: Faster in the gap, though less water would get through each tide
Slower, because less water could squeeze through the gap
No change, because the tide outside is the same as before
items.why: The bay behind keeps up less well, so the level difference across the gap grows and drives a faster current, while the smaller opening passes less volume.

items.ask: Why does Deception Pass reach eight knots only on some days?
choices: Only the biggest tides, near springs and on the larger tide of the day, make a big enough level difference
Eight knots needs a strong westerly wind to push water in from the Strait
The pass runs at eight knots only when the Skagit River is in flood
items.why: A bigger tide outside means a bigger difference across the gap, and the speed follows the difference.

items.ask: Why is the current in Admiralty Inlet a different kind of current from Deception Pass's?
choices: The inlet is a wide door, so the levels on each side stay close and the current is the volume the Sound needs to fill
The inlet is fresh water from the rivers, which flows out steadily whatever the tide is doing
The inlet has no tide of its own, so its current is driven only by the wind
items.why: In a big doorway the basin keeps up with the sea, so there is little fall across it; the current is the Sound filling and emptying through the opening.

items.ask: A kayaker plans to cross Deception Pass at slack water. Which is the best guide?
choices: The current prediction for the pass, because slack there comes at a different time from high water
The tide table for the nearest town, because slack always falls at high or low water
Any time in the early morning, because tidal currents are weakest at dawn
items.why: At a narrows slack is set by the level difference, not by high water, so the times can be an hour or more apart.

whidbey.title: Joseph Whidbey
whidbey.text: Whidbey was the *Discovery*'s master, the officer in charge of navigation, and did much of the expedition's surveying from its boats. Back in England he became an engineer, and with John Rennie he built the great breakwater across Plymouth Sound, begun in 1812.

knot.title: Knots
knot.text: A knot is one nautical mile an hour, 1.852 km/h, or about half a metre a second. Sailors once measured speed by letting a log on a line run out behind the ship for a set time and counting the knots tied along the line as they slipped over the stern.

torricelli.title: Falling water
torricelli.text: Evangelista Torricelli showed in the 1640s that water spouting from a hole a depth *h* below the surface leaves at about √(2*gh*), the speed of something dropped from that height. The same rule, with a correction for friction, gives the speed through a gap with a level difference *h* across it.

mixed.title: One tide in the model
mixed.text: The model uses one plain tide, the same size every half day. The real tide in the Salish Sea is mixed (lesson 9), so the two floods and two ebbs of a day differ, and so do the currents and the gaps between high water and slack.
